newsitem.title: UK: Export hopes underpin slow Europe grains market.
newsitem.headline: Export hopes underpin slow Europe grains market.

text.p: Hopes that the export market will improve before too much longer were the main supportive factor in a drifting European grains market, traders said.
Warmer weather has eased the transport problems of a week ago, as well as put an end to any fears that crops might be damaged by extreme cold.
French wheat prices drifted this week but recovered some ground on Thursday as a dreary export picture showed signs of brightening up.
The main pressure on wheat early in the week was reselling as operators awaited wheat tenders launched by Algeria and Iraq.

But dealers said news Algeria bought twice the tonnage of wheat it had tendered for was supportive. Algeria bought 150,000 tonnes of soft wheat, including 125,000 tonnes of French wheat under a Coface-guaranteed export credit.
Then sellers went to ground on Thursday on speculation that Iraq may have bought 200,000 tonnes, possibly from France.
Wheat into Rouen for January delivery was quoted at 857.50 per tonne on Thursday against 855 francs on Wednesday, but down five francs from levels a week ago.
The market however ignored bids to export 576,000 tonnes of EU soft wheat at rebates ranging from 13.80 to 17.87 Ecus per tonne at this week's EU grain auction.
Dealers described the wheat bids as "not aggressive", meaning they had expected exporters to come up with lower refund offers in view of firm world prices and a higher dollar.
Barley prices were broadly unchanged, with exporters seeming to hold back before covering recent sales to Saudi Arabia.
Maize prices wobbled early in the week but recovered, helped by better demand from the domestic starch industry and from importers in Portugal and the UK.
German wheat markets were quietly steady but a lack of consumer buying interest was expected to weigh on prices, brokers said.
Feed wheat demand was high and transport surcharges during the cold spell earlier this month had temporarily buoyed prices, but this strength had failed to spill over into bread wheat.
Warmer weather looked set to free up transport, and barge shipments to compound feed plants might resume soon.
Eastern European export prospects steadied prices as Mecklenburg state traders reported some sales to Poland.
Uzbek business was also expected for February/March.
The British market "seems to be bumping along the bottom," one trader said. An easier sterling Thursday is helping prices, but export business, healthy until the end of December, is still poor.
Traders were watching a Norwegian tender with interest. Norway bought 9,000 tonnes of wheat on Thursday, and some of it was likely to come from the UK, as well as Denmark and Germany.
British farmers appear relaxed about selling, traders said.
Spanish dealers said feed, milling and durum wheat ex-farm prices held firm in the week to January 16.
Spanish feed wheat has become scarce and dealers pointed out that few farmers now hold wheat of feed quality. Buyers opt for other more competitive grains for feed, they added.
Barley prices were also unchanged.
Maize prices eased slightly, pressured by cheaper imports from countries outside the European Union.

However this depressing influence was counteracted by a halt in the harvest in some areas due to the recent torrential rains and snow. Dealers said the Castilla y Leon and Aragon regions were worst hit.

Dealers continue to await information on U.S. imports. U.S. prices are expected to be slightly more competitive than those in Spain. Some said they expected to have more information at the end of the month.
Italian cereal prices were largely unchanged from a week ago as producers still have a lot of crop in their warehouses which prevent prices from rising much.
